definition: Willing to act dishonestly in exchange for money or other rewards.
example: A venal art appraiser would call a forged painting genuine for the right fee.
nuance: Venal means open to bribery, while the look-alike venial describes a small fault that is easily forgiven.
prompt: A building inspector is reviewing a newly built apartment complex.
options: The venal inspector signed off on cracked beams once the developer paid him.
The venal inspector refused a gift basket and failed the building for its missing fire exits.
The venal inspector made only a small, forgivable slip when he misspelled the street name.
The venal inspector, honored for forty years of loyal service, gave a speech at the ceremony.
reasons: Approving unsafe work because he was paid shows judgment that can be bought.
Turning down gifts and enforcing the rules shows integrity, the reverse of venality.
A minor, pardonable error is venial; venal involves selling one's honesty.
Being respected for long service suggests venerable, a different word entirely.

practice.prompt: Judges at a county baking contest are choosing who wins first prize.
options: One venal judge simply loved chocolate, so she ranked the fudge cake highest every year.
One venal judge gave the blue ribbon to a baker who had slipped her fifty dollars.
One venal judge returned a baker's bribe and scored every pie strictly on taste.
One venal judge felt guilty about a tiny mistake: she forgot to taste a single scone.
reasons: Favoring a flavor is personal bias, not trading her judgment for a reward.
Letting cash decide the winner means her vote was for sale.
Rejecting payment and judging fairly is incorruptible behavior.
A trivial, forgivable lapse would be venial; no bribe or dishonesty is involved.
